Foppery means excessive, ridiculous vanity about one's clothes, appearance, and manners — combined with a shallowness that makes a person care more about looking impressive than about anything of real substance. It also carries a second, related meaning: any foolish, trivial affectation or pretentious nonsense, whether about clothes or not.
Start Here: What Is a Fop?

To understand foppery, you first need to picture a fop. A fop is a man (historically the word was used for men, but the idea applies broadly) who is obsessed — truly, ridiculously obsessed — with fashion, personal appearance, and affected manners. He spends three hours choosing which coat to wear. He speaks in an overly elegant, artificial way. He admires himself constantly. He treats the choice of a hat as though it were a matter of life and death. He cares intensely about surfaces and not at all about depth.

Crucially, the fop's vanity has gone past normal care about appearance into something laughable. People around him find him silly, shallow, and a little absurd.

Foppery is the name for all of that — the behavior, the attitude, the whole package.

Foppery has a few qualities baked into it simultaneously. Understanding each one will sharpen your grasp of the word.

Excess. Foppery isn't simply caring about how you look. Everyone does that to some degree. Foppery is caring about it way too much — to a degree that most people around you find ridiculous and disproportionate. The excess is what makes it foppery rather than just grooming or style.

Affectation. An affectation is when someone puts on a manner, style, or behavior that isn't natural to them — they're performing a version of themselves that seems more refined, elegant, or impressive than they really are. A fop doesn't just dress extravagantly; he performs elegance. His gestures, his speech, his whole presentation is a kind of theatrical show. Foppery is soaked in this quality of artificiality.

Triviality. A fop treats trivial things as deeply important. He agonizes over the color of his gloves. He is offended if someone doesn't notice his new coat. Foppery is the act of pouring serious emotional energy into things that simply don't deserve it.

Shallowness. Beneath all the fuss about appearances, there is very little substance. Foppery is the enemy of depth, seriousness, and real character. It is all surface and no core.

Sense 1 — A type of behavior:
Foppery refers to the habit or practice of behaving like a fop. "His foppery was on full display at the dinner party — he spent twenty minutes explaining why his cufflinks were superior to everyone else's."

Sense 2 — A foolish, trivial thing or belief:
Foppery can also refer to a specific piece of nonsense, a silly affectation, or a trivial pretension — not just a pattern of behavior but a particular instance of foolishness. Shakespeare used it this way in King Lear, when a character dismisses the popular belief that the stars control your destiny as "the excellent foppery of the world" — meaning: what a ridiculous, foolish piece of nonsense people believe.

In this second sense, foppery just means foolish twaddle or empty, pretentious rubbish — and it doesn't have to be about clothes at all.

When someone uses the word "foppery," they are almost always being dismissive and mocking. It is not a neutral description. Calling someone's behavior "foppery" is a way of saying: this is silly, this is shallow, this is beneath serious consideration. It has a slightly contemptuous edge — the speaker is looking down at the behavior they're describing.

Because of this tone, the word is often used with a kind of dry, amused wit. When a no-nonsense character in a novel brushes aside all the concern about fashionable dress by calling it "mere foppery," they're signaling that they have more important things to think about.

This is important for sharpening the definition.

Foppery is not simply being well-dressed or stylish. A person can care deeply about fashion, dress beautifully, and have genuine taste — without any foppery. The fop doesn't just dress well; he makes an embarrassing spectacle of it.

Foppery is not elegance or refinement. True elegance has a quiet confidence and substance behind it. Foppery is a performance of elegance that lacks the real thing underneath.

Foppery is not just vanity in general. Vanity is the broader word for excessive pride in oneself. Foppery is vanity of a very specific, particular kind — the kind focused on clothing, appearance, affected manners, and surface impressions.
When Will You Encounter This Word?

Foppery is an old-fashioned, literary word. It was very much alive in the 17th, 18th, and early 19th centuries, when the "fop" was a well-known social type and a favorite figure of fun in plays and novels. You will most commonly encounter it in classic literature — Shakespeare, Restoration comedies, Jane Austen's era, and similar works.

In modern everyday speech, it is rare. When a contemporary writer or speaker uses it, they usually do so for deliberate effect — either to sound wittily old-fashioned, to add a literary flavor to their writing, or to mock something with a word that has centuries of contempt built into it.

"The general had no patience for the young officer's foppery — he wanted soldiers, not fashion plates."

"She rolled her eyes at the foppery of it all: three men debating for an hour over which color of pocket square was more distinguished."

"Dismiss such foppery from your mind — the stars do not determine your choices. You do."

"His foppery was legendary in the village; he was once seen returning home to change his hat because a cloud had altered the light."

Foppery is the ridiculous, excessive, and shallow obsession with one's appearance, clothing, and affected manners — or, more broadly, any trivial, pretentious foolishness — and the word is always used with a tone of mockery and dismissal.
